This paper aims to bridge the gap between the design specification document from CPSLO and traditional satellite design practices, such as iterative design and systems engineering approaches.

Most of the features of the software and CubeSat are shown with place holders for actual interconnections within the model. These can be edited and updated later as needed. Further development of the model for the collaborative project is intended to be done with a larger team in the future.
Objective 1: Create a standardized systems engineering model for CubeSat designers and developers as a basis to construct their satellites from.

The collaboration project above involves the design and development of a 3U CubeSat, by CPP students and staff. This CubeSat will incorporate a new thermal technology, proposed by several JPL technologists, and will be manufactured using additive manufacturing techniques on several of the CubeSat subsystems using AFRL facilities.

The complexity of the project required the usage of systems engineering methodologies to address requirements tracking and documentation, subsystem designs, and system operational parameters including the life cycle of the CubeSat. To obtain concise data and design parameters and decisions, MBSE was a necessary practice for the project.

The enthusiasm from the collaborators bolstered the potential of it from being a single project to a multi-project program, as such the need for a documented model that is easily modifiable for changing project goals is needed for the CubeSat Technology Exploration Program (CubeSTEP) to continue in the coming years.

To achieve this, the MBSE program Cameo Enterprise Architecture (CEA) from No Magic at Dassault Systemes is used to design the model-based design of the satellite and its supporting elements. The application of this software and a supporting add-on called SysML from No Magic is described in the remaining sections of the paper.

Due to the limitations of time, personnel, access to the SysML software capabilities, this constrained the level of fidelity of the designed CubeSat model. As such the model diagrams described in the remaining sections are based on the availability of the resources at hand as well as the knowledge of the software acquired during its development.

Thus, the scope of the model was restricted to high and medium level modeling where overall system properties and elements like requirements development as well as the detailed subsystem design were implemented. However, intricate modeling of component interconnections and detailed software processing and sequencing was limited.

The model diagrams in the next sections are the results of combining satellite design practices (Larson and Wertz; Helvajian and Janson; Fortescue et al.), system life cycle Information, as well as referencing the work done by the INCOSE SSWG (Kaslow et al.; Spangelo et al.).

The major elements of the model show above describe a majority of the life cycle elements involved in the design of a satellites and its mission, including conceptual development, system definition, system design, and into satellite operations.

However, to ensure the usage of this MBSE design for CubeSats in general, many of the systems and diagrams were design with generalities and optional functions that may not be used in every mission, such as deployable mechanisms and propulsion subsystems.
Following the same guidelines as traditional project development, the system stakeholders were determined first including their involvement within the CubeSTEP project.

The requirements of the system are then defined from the needs of the stakeholders of CubeSTEP. After compiling each entity's needs into Table 1, the system requirements were developed with these baseline needs in mind for the project goals.

After developing the life cycle and mission level requirements as well as the subsystem design requirements for the CubeSTEP, a requirements table was generated in SysML for ease of tracking, verifications, and control. The table provides users with the ability to direct requirements to specific design parameters and analyses within the system model.

With the intention of the CubeSat model being used beyond just the CubeSTEP missions, the subsystem general requirements were compiled from CubeSat Design Specifications, CubeSat 101, and the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook into the respective subsystem requirements diagrams (Lan; Chin et al.; Hirshorn).

Similarly, the remaining requirements of the CubeSat model were developed with general form and standardized requirements in the documents listed previously. Several subsystem requirements were adjusted to address the needs and goals of the CubeSTEP project.
One example is the modification of the CubeSTEP Attitude Control System Requirements correlating it to the pointing accuracy needed for the CubeSat's power and communication systems, shown below.
After the CubeSat's requirements development was completed and thoroughly modeled within the SysML software, the design for the various subsystem component diagrams were begun.

It is also noteworthy that the model is capable of showing alternative design decisions in the same diagram, such as Figure 14's optional component pathways of the body-mounted and two-axis gimbled solar panel configurations. This allowed for the model to accommodate both design choices while still providing the engineering team with alternative architectures to develop with.

To increase the accessibility and ease of use of the model for non systems engineers, diagram hyperlinks were implements into the subsystem BDDs connecting them to their respective requirements diagrams as well as their Internal Block Diagram.

Using the previously design BDDs of the CubeSTEP's subsystems allows modelers to reduce the time needed to create an IBD by automatically generating the predefined information from their BDD, providing the bare-bone structure of an IBD leaving the modeler to create the connection and data flow lines in the diagram.

Combining the requirements, use cases, block definition, and internal block diagrams discussed in this section, the generalized CubeSat architecture model is formed. These diagrams enable future CubeSat model users the ability to quickly modify, determine, and distribute structural information of the satellite within the model and to the engineering teams designing the hardware and bus segments of the CubeSat.

The various modes that the CubeSat transitions through and the operations carried out within them are best envisioned in the SysML State Machine diagram (STM). Figure 25 below fully describes the states of the CubeSTEP for its operational life cycle.

SysML makes up for this with its capability of integration with external software, such as MATLAB, STK, Python, and more. The ability to call functions and simulations from these more robust analytical software and use the resulting information in SysML enables the modelers and engineering teams to conduct larger scale simulations of a CubeSat's performance as well as tracking for data validation and requirements compliance.

Applying the block definition diagrams, failure modes of a satellite are created by displaying the failure constraints causing a mission failure. As shown in Figure 28, each failure mode is then correlated to a respective activity block, linked to one of the activity diagrams discussed earlier.

The creation of the constraints above allows for the user to generate parametric diagrams for each of the failures to conduct the analyses necessary for determining the system reliability. Using additional features of SysML Parametric diagrams enables the automatic generation of Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) tables as needed.
Each major subsystem, such as Figure 31 and Figure 32, and the overarching CubeSat, Figure 30, have modeled in fault trees in preparation for the analysis of the subsystems and overall architecture.

Each fault tree must then be run through a cut set minimization, where a cut set is a set of occurrences that would cause a system failure. The minimum cut set removes the redundant cuts from the fault tree reducing the necessary work for reliability analysis while keeping its integrity.

These failure analysis methods provide the engineers and development team with insightful information on the high-risk areas of a design and where to focus efforts to improve the system reliability before operations.

The implementation of the CubeSat model described above to CPP's CubeSTEP, adds to the viability of the model's usage in CubeSat design. Having the CubeSTEP design team use portions of the model, such as the requirements listing, behavioral sequences, and preliminary calculations used by the structures, thermal, and systems engineering teams reveals the importance of having a system model capable of providing team members with information when necessary.

Beyond the design team's usage of the model, our stakeholders from NASA JPL and US AFRL were able to convey the mission objectives and correlate any specific requirements needed. The verification and satisfaction of their needs was presented to them through the requirements tables and listings described within this paper.

Having a standardized formulation for the design and development of CubeSats, specifically through the generalized model designed here, will lead to greater reliability and performance of the satellites in the future of all form factors.
